title: Authors have no way to ask for a higher or lower pixel density than the browser's default when selecting from `srcset`

labels.name: needs implementer interest
labels.description: Moving the issue forward requires implementers to express interest

body: ### What problem are you trying to solve? When a browser selects a candidate from a `w`-descriptor `srcset`, it targets roughly 1 image pixel per device pixel of the source size resolved from `sizes`. That target is fixed. Authors can describe layout (`sizes`), art direction (``), and the candidates on offer (`srcset`), but cannot say "for this image, aim higher than the default" or "aim lower". The only knob that moves the result is `sizes`, and `sizes` is supposed to describe geometry, not intent. Quality vs. bytes is a per-image tradeoff that goes both ways: - **Fetch less.** Below-the-fold, decorative, or secondary images on a 3x phone fetch ~9x the pixels of a 1x image for content the user may never look at closely. The author would take 0.75x or 0.5x and spend the bytes on LCP instead. - **Fetch more.** Images the user will pinch-zoom or that the page enlarges in place (CSS `transform: scale`, a lightbox), or that carry fine detail (maps, line art, screenshots). Page zoom already re-selects because it changes `devicePixelRatio`; pinch-zoom and scripted zoom deliberately do not change it, so nothing ever re-selects for them. The browser cannot infer any of this. It does not know which images are decorative, which are the product, or which will be zoomed. Those are author decisions with nowhere to go. ### What solutions exist today? **Lie in `sizes`.** Inflate or shrink `sizes` so the browser targets a different candidate. It is the only lever and it has real costs: - It is incompatible with `sizes="auto"` (#4654). You cannot say "auto" and "but 1.5x more" at the same time. - Once #13046 lands, `naturalWidth` is derived from `sizes`, so a dishonest `sizes` yields a wrong `naturalWidth` (related: #12565, #6532). The workaround now corrupts a DOM API. - `(min-resolution)` queries in `sizes` and `x` descriptors do not help: still a lie about layout, per-breakpoint rather than per-image, and neither composes with `auto`. **Prior discussion.** #4421 (open) asks for a density *cap* to protect high-DPR users (`maxresolution` / `maxdpr`; #5901 proposes a UA-side cap note). The objection was that protecting users from over-fetching is the UA's job. That objection does not apply here: this is author intent the UA cannot know, in either direction, not a user-protection default. The UA keeps its freedom to clamp. ### How would you solve it? Illustrative only; the problem matters more than the shape. A content attribute on `img` (and `source`), a positive number, default `1`, that multiplies the device pixel ratio used for candidate selection. Applied *after* the source size is computed, so it composes with `sizes="auto"` and leaves `sizes` honest. ```html ``` In [select an image source from a source set](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/images.html#select-an-image-source-from-a-source-set), the implementation-defined choice is made against `devicePixelRatio × densityscale`. First example: a 2x, 800px-wide viewport targets 1200 image px instead of 1600, about 44% fewer pixels. Second: a 600px box on a 1x screen targets 900 instead of 600. Whatever the final syntax: - **A multiplier, not an absolute.** `0.75` means the same thing on a 1x laptop and a 3x phone. Absolute DPR targets do not port across devices, which is where #4421 got stuck. - **A hint.** Selection stays implementation-defined. UAs may clamp or ignore it under Save-Data, low memory, or their own density cap. - **Orthogonal to everything else.** No change to `sizes` parsing, the preload scanner, or `naturalWidth`/`currentSrc` semantics. It only changes *which* candidate is chosen. - **Naming is open.** The name should say "multiplier". ### Anything else? Airbnb would use this immediately: lower density on secondary imagery to cut bytes and protect LCP, higher on the few images users zoom. We do this today by lying in `sizes`, and have no fix once we move to `sizes="auto"`. cc @zcorpan @noamr @eeeps @yoavweiss
